The Ten Examples of the Difficulty of Human Birth

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who bears extremely pure omniscient knowledge, and I explain through ten examples how difficult it is to obtain human birth.

The ten examples are: 1. Chollak (the blind man and the lame man), 2. Passa (the dice), 3. Dhanya (the grain), 4. Jua (the gamble), 5. Ratna (the jewel), 6. Swapna (the dream), 7. Chakra (the wheel), 8. Kachhua (the turtle), 9. Yug (the cosmic cycle), and 10. Paramanu (the atom).

1. Chollak: After Lord Neminath attained nirvana, Brahmadata became the twelfth Chakravartin in Ayodhya. He had a brave vassal named Sahasrabhat. Sahasrabhat's wife Sumitra had a son named Vasudev. Vasudev was neither educated nor qualified for royal service. Therefore, after his father's death, he could not get his father's position, which was a respectable post. And truly, without acquiring some qualification, one cannot gain honour in royal service.

His mother was very sad at his condition, but the poor woman was helpless. Due to poverty, she took shelter in an old, fallen hut and began to make ends meet somehow. She started using Vasudev for some work with future hope. She began sending him to nearby villages with a basket containing laddoos, pedas, paan, etc., so that Vasudev would learn some hard work and become somewhat clever. By doing this, Sumitra succeeded, and Vasudev learned something. He no longer liked sitting idle as before. Sumitra then got Vasudev appointed as the king's bodyguard through some connection.

One day, the Chakravartin went outside the city on horseback for a breath of fresh air. The horse he rode was very unruly. With just a slight touch of the heel, it carried the Chakravartin away like the wind. Going very far, it dropped him in a terrible, fearsome forest. At this time, the Chakravartin was in great distress. His life was flickering with hunger and thirst.

Readers will remember that his bodyguard Vasudev had been made clever by his mother in walking, running, and rushing. This was why, when the Chakravartin's horse ran away with him, Vasudev also ran after him at top speed, carrying some food and drink. The Chakravartin had been sitting in the forest for about three-quarters of an hour when Vasudev arrived and saved him.

This story illustrates how rare and precious human birth is. Just as Vasudev's mother's efforts led to his ability to save the king, so too must we use our human birth wisely through hard work and good deeds. The ten examples collectively show that human birth is as difficult to obtain as a blind man and lame man cooperating to climb a tree, as a dice landing on the right number, as grain growing in perfect conditions, as winning a gamble, as finding a jewel, as a meaningful dream, as a wheel turning correctly, as a turtle surfacing in a vast ocean, as the rare alignment of cosmic cycles, and as atoms coming together in perfect order. The wise should use this precious human birth for spiritual progress.
